item.text:
**Bottom Line**
Tshisekedi’s 2024 use of security powers looks mostly coercive rather than narrowly lawful. The clearest pattern is emergency-style militarization, punitive deterrence, and weak due process. There is some limited positive evidence of administrative stabilization efforts like P-DDRCS and command reshuffles, but I found no strong evidence of a rights-constraining framework for emergency powers or anti-terror controls.

**Accepted Claims**
- **DRC President Felix Tshisekedi must be held accountable for human rights violations** | **Amnesty International** | **2024-09-30** | [source](https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2024/09/drc-president-felix-tshisekedi-must-be-held-accountable-for-human-rights-violations/)  
  Amnesty says the ongoing “State of Siege” in North Kivu and Ituri militarized everyday life and concentrated power in military and police officials, while a crackdown on dissent proceeded under the pretext of defending the country against enemies. This is the clearest evidence that emergency-style controls were being used as tools of coercion.  
  **IDs:** `3B.5`, `3B.1`, `3B.2`, `3B.4`

- **2024 Country Reports on Human Rights Practices: Democratic Republic of the Congo** | **U.S. Department of State via ECOI** | **2024** | [source](https://www.ecoi.net/en/document/2128488.html)  
  The report says security services used unofficial detention facilities and did not reliably observe arrest, detention, and due-process rules. That is strong evidence that administrative controls and security powers were not being used narrowly or lawfully.  
  **IDs:** `3B.5`, `3B.1`, `3B.2`, `3B.4`

- **DRC: Reinstating executions shows a callous disregard for human rights** | **Amnesty International** | **2024-03-15** | [source](https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2024/03/drc-reinstating-executions-shows-a-callous-disregard-for-human-rights/)  
  Amnesty says the government reinstated executions to combat armed groups and gang violence, but that this was a huge step backward and a dangerous response in a weak justice system. This is strong evidence of punitive coercion rather than lawful restraint.  
  **IDs:** `3B.5`, `3B.1`, `3B.2`

- **Congo lifts moratorium on death penalty, justice ministry circular shows** | **Reuters** | **2024-03-15** | [source](https://www.yahoo.com/news/congo-lifts-moratorium-death-penalty-153836346.html)  
  Reuters reports the move was framed as a way to rid the army of traitors and curb terrorism and banditry. That indicates the government was using anti-terror and disciplinary powers as hardline punishment tools, not as narrowly tailored safeguards.  
  **IDs:** `3B.5`, `3B.1`, `3B.2`

- **DRC: Human rights priorities for the government of Democratic Republic of Congo during President Tshisekedi’s second term** | **Amnesty International** | **2024-06-24** | [source](https://www.amnesty.org/en/documents/afr62/8155/2024/en/)  
  Amnesty says the government had made little to no progress on previous human-rights pledges and highlighted the need to end the state of siege, fix prisons, and stop arbitrary detention. This is useful as a high-level negative assessment of security-governance legality.  
  **IDs:** `3B.5`, `3B.4`, `3B.1`, `3B.2`

- **Programme de désarmement et démobilisation: une alternative pour la paix et la cohésion sociale** | **ACP** | **2024-03-22** | [source](https://acp.cd/nation/programme-de-desarmement-et-demobilisation-une-alternative-pour-la-paix-et-la-cohesion-sociale/)  
  The government described P-DDRCS as a stabilization and cohesion program meant to restore state authority where absent. This is the best limited positive evidence I found: a civilian stabilization instrument rather than purely coercive control.  
  **IDs:** `3B.5`, `2B.5`, `2B.7`

- **Army disarray hobbles Congo's fight with Rwanda-backed rebels, officers say** | **Reuters** | **2024-07-17** | [source](https://theprint.in/world/army-disarray-hobbles-congos-fight-with-rwanda-backed-rebels-officers-say/2160048/)  
  Reuters says the government relied on Wazalendo militias, had no control over them, and faced weak discipline and poor logistics; Tshisekedi reportedly told them to be brought in line. This is mixed evidence, but the reliance on uncontrolled proxies is the key negative signal for lawful, narrow use of administrative force.  
  **IDs:** `3B.5`, `2B.5`, `3B.2`, `3B.4`

- **Congolese president sacks military top brass in major reshuffle** | **Reuters** | **2024-12-20** | [source](https://theprint.in/world/congolese-president-sacks-military-top-brass-in-major-reshuffle/2411531/)  
  Tshisekedi replaced the army chief, military intelligence head, and many senior officers, with Reuters noting the reshuffle was framed as boosting efficiency. This is the strongest late-year corrective move I found, but it reads more like damage control than a clear rights-protecting reform of emergency powers.  
  **IDs:** `3B.5`, `3B.4`, `2B.9`

- **World Report 2024: Democratic Republic of Congo** | **Human Rights Watch** | **2024** | [source](https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/democratic-republic-congo)  
  HRW says government forces killed civilians during enforcement operations and repression against journalists, activists, critics, and opposition members continued. That supports the view that security and administrative controls were used for intimidation and coercive control, not just lawful protection.  
  **IDs:** `3B.5`, `3B.1`, `3B.2`, `3B.4`

**Search Gap**
I found no strong evidence of a narrowly tailored, rights-constraining emergency-powers framework in 2024. The few positive items were limited to stabilization programs and personnel reshuffles; they do not outweigh the broader pattern of militarized emergency rule, punitive measures, and weak due process.
